objectives.statement: Structure a strict, accessible heading hierarchy from h1 down without skipping levels.
Apply semantic emphasis (strong, em) to indicate importance and vocal stress rather than purely visual formatting.

content.title: Outlining Documents with Headings and Text
content.hook: When you pick up a newspaper or a textbook, your eyes scan big headlines and section titles before reading paragraphs. On the web, headings create that vital outline for sighted users, search engines, and screen readers alike.
content.context: HTML provides six levels of headings (`<h1>` through `<h6>`). Sighted users see font sizes change, but assistive technologies use headings to build a navigable table of contents. Never choose a heading tag based on its visual size; choose it based on document hierarchy.
goals: Establish a clear document outline with one primary `<h1>` and nested subheadings.
Avoid skipping heading levels (e.g., jump from `<h2>` directly to `<h4>`).
Differentiate semantic emphasis (`<strong>`, `<em>`) from visual styling (`<b>`, `<i>`).

content.title: Document Heading Hierarchy
content.description: Level 1: <h1> Page Title -> Level 2: <h2> Major Section -> Level 3: <h3> Subsection. Screen readers present this tree as a navigable outline.

content.prompt: A developer wants small text for a subsection title, so they write `<h5>` directly beneath an `<h1>` without any `<h2>`, `<h3>`, or `<h4>`. What is the primary problem with this markup?
content.code:

options: The browser throws a fatal error and refuses to display the paragraph.
It breaks the document outline for screen reader users by skipping heading levels 2, 3, and 4.
HTML only allows headings if they are placed inside a `<head>` tag.
The `<h5>` tag is deprecated and removed in HTML5.

validation.expected: It breaks the document outline for screen reader users by skipping heading levels 2, 3, and 4.

feedback.correct: Spot on! Skipping heading levels creates a confusing outline in assistive technology. If you need smaller text, use the correct heading level (e.g., `<h2>`) and style it with CSS.
feedback.incorrect: Headings represent hierarchical document structure. Skipping levels confuses screen readers. Visual size must always be controlled via CSS.

content.prompt: Explain the difference between using `<strong>` versus `<b>`, and `<em>` versus `<i>`. Why should developers favor semantic tags over visual styling tags?

feedback.correct: Excellent! `<strong>` and `<em>` convey semantic importance and emphasis to screen readers and browsers, whereas `<b>` and `<i>` are purely historical visual decorations with no semantic weight.
feedback.incorrect: Focus on the distinction between semantic meaning (understood by screen readers and machines) and visual appearance (styling).

content.title: Key Takeaways: Headings and Text
takeaways: Headings create a navigable hierarchy (`<h1>` down to `<h6>`); never skip heading levels.
A page should generally have exactly one `<h1>` that describes the main subject.

Use `

` for paragraph blocks; browsers automatically handle flow and margin.
Use `<strong>` for high importance and `<em>` for stress emphasis; use CSS for purely visual bolding and italics.
